human_tolerance.notes: The article says the species is now common in many urban areas because the structure of tall buildings and houses resembles the cliffs of its original habitat, and that it may nest in residential areas, breeding in roofs and apertures and under house eaves. It is also described as a pest in some areas, raiding orchards and attacking people who wander too close to their nests.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: A cliff nester that is commonly double-brooded, laying two to four (usually three) blue eggs spotted with red-brown and incubating for 13-14 days, with a further 22-28 days to fledge. The source gives no calendar window, so the phase covers the year.

phases.name: flocking
phases.note: When not breeding the species is highly gregarious and associates with large flocks of its own kind; the territorial nesting phase covers the remaining individuals.

vocalizations.description: A number of whistled calls, of which the most familiar is the contact call transcribed in the source as 'cher-leeeoo'.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 5230739 from the species/match endpoint and iNaturalist taxon 204554 from the taxa endpoint; the Wikidata QID is the one the English article's taxobox links to.

conservation.note: The species article's taxobox records IUCN category Least Concern, and the text states 'The red-winged starling is not endangered'.

range.note: The article gives the range as running 'down eastern Africa from Ethiopia to the Cape of Good Hope, KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng in South Africa'. Only the two endpoints the source names are recorded, rather than filling in the intermediate countries the source does not list.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: The article describes the bird flying between cliffs, perching on livestock and game, and taking insects and ectoparasites from animals in the manner of oxpeckers, so Walk and Fly are both recorded.

traits.nest_type.note: 'This starling is a cliff nester, breeding on rocky cliffs, outcrops and gorges', building a lined nest of grass and twigs with a mud base on a ledge; in towns it uses roofs, apertures and eaves.

traits.perching.note: 'Red-winged starlings are often spotted perching on livestock and game', and it chooses robust racemes to perch on when taking nectar.

traits.mass_kg.note: AVONET Mass 132.9 g for Onychognathus morio, sourced by AVONET to Dunning.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Authored bracket of 100-170 g around the AVONET mean, allowing for the sex difference the article notes, the female having a grey head and being generally lighter. No sourced mass range was found; treat as an estimate.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of the male's 27-30 cm, rounded to 0.285 m.

traits.wingspan_m.note: Twice the AVONET Wing.Length of 153.9 mm, rounded to 0.308 m. AVONET does not give a wingspan directly.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Honest gap. Neither the species article, Wikidata nor GBIF gives a longevity figure for this species, and no openly licensed source with one was found. 10 years is an authored placeholder for a large starling; it is not a sourced value.

traits.diet.note: 'Like other starlings, the red-winged starling is an omnivore, taking a wide range of seeds, berries, nectar from plants such as Aloe and Schotia brachypetala, and invertebrates', plus nestlings and adults of other birds, and 'it will also scavenge on carrion and human food scrap'. The 0.3/0.25/0.2/0.15/0.1 split is authored from that list; the source gives no proportions.

traits.senses.note: Authored: diurnal passerine with coloured vision and modest olfaction.

traits.social.note: 'The red-winged starling is territorial, aggressive and intolerant when nesting' but 'when not breeding, red-winged starlings are highly gregarious and will associate with other members of their species in large flocks'. The upper bound of 60 is authored; the source says 'large flocks' without a number.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Recorded as diurnal: an active daytime bird, with no nocturnal behaviour described.

traits.defense.note: Mob. 'It is territorial, aggressive and intolerant when nesting, and will attack other species, including domestic animals and humans.'

traits.wariness.note: Very low, from the same passage: the bird attacks people who wander too close to its nests and is described as a pest that raids orchards, rather than keeping its distance.

habitat.use.note: AVONET classifies the habitat as Rock with an insessorial lifestyle, matching the article's cliff nesting. The 0.45 arboreal / 0.4 aerial / 0.15 ground split is authored from a bird that flies widely between cliffs, perches high on livestock and trees, and comes down to forage and to raid scraps.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Derived from the nest sites the article gives: rocky cliffs, outcrops and gorges, and in towns roofs, apertures and house eaves.

habitat.resources.note: The five food tags map one to one onto the omnivore sentence in the article, and the cavity nesting tag onto the cliff and roof nesting sites. Weights are authored.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Exploiter, dist_building_min_m and uses_gardens are all sourced from the passage on urban expansion into cities and towns and nesting in roofs, apertures and house eaves. impervious_max and road_mortality are authored.

seasonal.strategy.note: The article describes no migration or dormancy for this species and places adults on cliffs in town all year, so ActiveYearRound is recorded by inference from the absence of any stated movement.

seasonal.phases.note: The article gives a 13-14 day incubation and 22-28 days to fledge, and says the species is commonly double-brooded, but gives no calendar months for breeding anywhere in the range. Rather than invent a window the source does not state, both phases span the year and are distinguished by a fraction.

seasonal.life_stages.note: 'The female incubates the eggs for 13-14 days, with another 22-28 days to fledge', rounded to 28 days for the juvenile duration; the 0.9 scale is authored.

vocalizations.song.note: 'This species has a number of whistled calls, but the most familiar is the contact call, cher-leeeoo.'

look.note: Male mainly iridescent black plumage with chestnut flight feathers that are particularly noticeable in flight; the female has an ash-grey head and upper breast; the juvenile resembles the male but is less glossy and has brown rather than dark red eyes. Proportions are authored.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program: a strongly perching, cliff-nesting omnivore that flies between feeding sites and suburbs, takes fruit, seeds, nectar and invertebrates, and nests on a ledge or in a roof void. The program wants both a song and an alarm call, and the source documents one set of whistled calls, so the same documented call serves both contexts.
